common_name: Oddity Hens and Chicks (Quilled Tubular-Leaf Sempervivum)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun; needs almost no soil depth and establishes quickly in rock crevices, troughs, or containers.

directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun; this novelty cultivar needs the same negligent, dry treatment as any hens and chicks and rots quickly in wet or heavy soil. Oddity is a conversation-piece sempervivum in which most leaves curl inward into narrow, quill-like tubes instead of forming a flat rosette, giving each 'hen' a spiky, sea-urchin appearance that is distinct from any typical hens and chicks cultivar; a few normal flat leaves usually mix in among the tubular ones. It spreads by the same short-stemmed offsets as other sempervivums, making it easy to multiply for troughs, crevice gardens, and collector containers. The parent rosette blooms once on a tall stalk after several years and then dies, leaving offsets to fill in.

common_name: Commander Hay Hens and Chicks (Large Purple-Centered Sempervivum)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun.

directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun, and remove faded rosettes after they bloom and die to keep the mat tidy. Commander Hay is one of the older, best-known large-rosette sempervivum cultivars, an Award of Garden Merit winner with broad, deep maroon-purple centers shading out to bright green leaf tips, giving mature clumps a striking two-toned, almost metallic look. Its bigger-than-average 4–5 inch rosettes make it a strong single-specimen focal point in rock gardens and alpine troughs, not just a filler groundcover, while it still spreads readily by offsets over time. Like all sempervivums it needs sharp drainage and full sun to hold its best color and dense form, fading and stretching in shade.

common_name: Pacific Blue Ice Hens and Chicks (Silvery-Blue Sempervivum)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun.

directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun; strong sun deepens the cool, frosty color this cultivar is grown for. Pacific Blue Ice is a Pacific hybridizer selection prized for its tight, symmetrical rosettes of powdery, silvery blue-gray leaves with a faint violet blush at the tips, a cooler, icier tone than the greens, reds, and purples typical of most hens and chicks. It offsets freely to form a slowly spreading mat, making it a good color-contrast companion to the warmer-toned sempervivum cultivars in a mixed trough or crevice planting. As with all sempervivums, sharp drainage is essential — the plant tolerates drought and poor soil far better than it tolerates wet feet.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, alkaline, gravelly or limestone-based soil in full sun.

directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; native to limestone scree in the French and Italian Alps, this species performs best where soil pH runs neutral to alkaline rather than acidic. Sempervivum calcareum forms neat, symmetrical blue-gray rosettes with distinctive dark maroon to blackish leaf tips that intensify in strong sun and cold weather, a color pattern that has made it a parent of many hybrid sempervivum cultivars grown today. It spreads slowly and modestly compared to more vigorous sempervivum hybrids, staying tidy in small crevice gardens, alpine troughs, and tufa plantings without swamping neighboring plants. Each rosette flowers once on a stout stalk after several years and then dies, leaving offsets behind to continue the clump.
